impish

IM-pish · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Impish is inclined to cause harmless trouble for fun.

The impish kitten kept batting pens off the desk just to watch them roll away.

Worked Example

With an impish grin, the boy swapped the salt and sugar shakers before dinner.

The prank was harmless and clearly done for fun rather than any real malice, which is exactly the playful mischief captured by impish.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mischievous: Mischievous is the broad, everyday word for playful troublemaking of any flavor. Impish narrows it: mischief with an elf-like, teasing charm, true to the imp it comes from -- a grin, a small surprise, never anything mean.

puckish: Puckish means playfully mischievous in a light, elfin spirit -- the word comes from Puck, Shakespeare's trickster sprite -- and like impish it never means real harm. Puckish leans bookish and whimsical, while impish suggests a naughtier, grinning energy.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

solemn: serious and dignified

Where it sits · how wicked the fun becomes — playful → impish → devilish

playful vs. impish: Being playful is simply lighthearted and fun; being impish adds a specific edge of harmless mischief-making.

devilish vs. impish: Impish mischief is charming and harmless; devilish mischief is wickedly, intentionally troublemaking.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — imp

root — imp: a small mischievous sprite or devil (Old English (impa))

suffix — -ish

suffix — -ish: having the character of (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Impish combines the noun imp -- an old folklore word for a small, mischievous sprite -- with -ish, 'having the character of,' so impish literally means 'sprite-like.'

Use the root in a new word: imp

Use the root in a new word: imp: Imp is a real standalone word on its own, still used today for a small mischievous creature or a playfully naughty child.
